Bush was critical of Cheney, describing him as: "He had his own empire there and marched to his own drummer. It just showed me that you cannot do it that way. The president should not have that worry," and that "The big mistake that was made was letting Cheney bring in kind of his own State Department."[228]

In popular culture  
A Dick Cheney impersonator at the 2010 Rally to Restore Sanity and/or Fear  
In Eminem's 2002 single "Without Me", where the lines "I know that you got a job, Ms. Cheney / But your husband's heart problem's complicating" refer to his health problems.[229]  
In The Day After Tomorrow, the character Raymond Becker (played by Kenneth Welsh) is intended to be a caricature of Dick Cheney.[230]  
In W. (2008), a biographical comedy-drama film directed by Oliver Stone, he is portrayed by Richard Dreyfuss.[231]  
In War Dogs (2016), where the line "God bless Dick Cheney's America" refers to his support of American military presence in Iraq.[232]  
In Who Is America? (2018), a political satire series, Sacha Baron Cohen pranked Cheney into signing a makeshift waterboard kit.[233]  
In Vice (2018), a biographical comedy-drama film written and directed by Adam McKay, Cheney is portrayed by Christian Bale,[234] for which the latter won a Golden Globe Award[235] and was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actor.[236]  
In Mrs. America (2020), a historical drama television miniseries produced by FX, Cheney is portrayed by Andrew Hodwitz.[237]  
Bob Rivers did a parody cover called "Cheney's Got a Gun"[238]  
Cheney has been compared to Darth Vader, a characterization originated by his critics, but which was later adopted humorously by Cheney himself as well as by members of his family and staff.[239]  
Personal life
Cheney was a member of the United Methodist Church and was the first Methodist vice president to serve under a Methodist president.[240] His brother, Bob, is a former civil servant at the Bureau of Land Management.[241]

His wife, Lynne, was chair of the National Endowment for the Humanities from 1986 to 1996. She is a public speaker, author, and a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.[242] They had two daughters, Elizabeth ("Liz") and Mary Cheney, and seven grandchildren. Liz, a former congresswoman from Wyoming, is married to Philip Perry, a former general counsel of the Department of Homeland Security. Mary, a former employee of the Colorado Rockies baseball team and the Coors Brewing Company, was a campaign aide to the Bush re-election campaign; she lives in Great Falls, Virginia, with her wife Heather Poe.[243] Cheney publicly supported gay marriage after leaving the vice presidency.[244]
Residences
Since 1993, Cheney owned a house in Teton County, Wyoming.[245] In 1987, Cheney purchased a house in McLean, Virginia for $450,000; he sold it to Joe Allbaugh in 2001 for $690,000.[246] In 2000, he sold a multimillion-dollar house in Dallas, where he lived while he was chairman of Halliburton.[246] In 2000, he acquired a lot in McLean for $1.35 million and filed plans to build a 21,000 square foot home.[246][247] In 2008, Cheney purchased a home on Chain Bridge Road in McLean, Virginia, which he tore down for a replacement structure to be built.[248] At the time of his death, the house had a market value of $5.8 million.[249] In 2019, he sold his vacation house in Saint Michaels, Maryland on Eastern Shore of Maryland for $2.1 million, at a loss; he had paid $2.67 million for the house in 2005.[250]
Health problems

Cheney's long histories of cardiovascular disease and periodic need for urgent health care raised questions of whether he was medically fit to serve in public office.[251] Having smoked approximately three packs of cigarettes per day for nearly 20 years,[252] Cheney had his first of five heart attacks on June 18, 1978,[253] at age 37. Subsequent heart attacks in 1984, 1988, 2000, and 2010 resulted in the moderate contractile dysfunction of his left ventricle.[254] He underwent four-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting in 1988, coronary artery stenting in November 2000, urgent coronary balloon angioplasty in March 2001, and the implantation of a implantable cardioverter-defibrillator in June 2001.[255]
On September 24, 2005, Cheney underwent a six-hour endo-vascular procedure to repair popliteal artery aneurysms bilaterally, a catheter treatment technique used in the artery behind each knee.[256] The condition was discovered at a regular physical in July, and was not life-threatening.[257] Cheney was hospitalized for tests after experiencing shortness of breath five months later. In late April 2006, an ultrasound revealed that the clot was smaller.[256]

On March 5, 2007, Cheney was treated for deep vein thrombosis in his left leg at George Washington University Hospital after experiencing pain in his left calf. Doctors prescribed blood-thinning medication and allowed him to return to work.[258] CBS News reported that during the morning of November 26, 2007, Cheney was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation and underwent treatment that afternoon.[256] On July 12, 2008, Cheney underwent a cardiology exam; doctors reported that his heartbeat was normal for a 67-year-old man with a history of heart problems. As part of his annual checkup, he was administered an electrocardiogram and radiological imaging of the stents placed in the arteries behind his knees in 2005. Doctors said that Cheney had not experienced any recurrence of atrial fibrillation and that his special pacemaker had neither detected nor treated any heart arrhythmia.[259] On October 15, 2008, Cheney returned to the hospital briefly to treat a minor irregularity.[260]
On January 19, 2009, Cheney strained his back "while moving boxes into his new house," according to a White House statement. As a consequence, he was in a wheelchair for two days, including his attendance at the 2009 United States presidential inauguration.[261][262] On February 22, 2010, Cheney was admitted to George Washington University Hospital after experiencing chest pains. A spokesperson later said Cheney had experienced a mild heart attack after doctors had run tests.[263] On June 25, 2010, Cheney was admitted to George Washington University Hospital after reporting discomfort.[264]
In early-July 2010, Cheney was outfitted with a left-ventricular assist device (LVAD) at Inova Fairfax Heart and Vascular Institute to compensate for worsening congestive heart failure.[265] The device pumped blood continuously through his body.[266][267] He was released from Inova on August 9, 2010,[268] and had to decide whether to seek a full heart transplant.[269][270] This pump was centrifugal and as a result he remained alive without a pulse for nearly 15 months.[271]

**Nelson Aldrich Rockefeller** (July 8, 1908 – January 26, 1979) was the 41st vice president of the United States, serving from 1974 to 1977 under President Gerald Ford. A member of the Republican Party and the wealthy Rockefeller family, he was the 49th governor of New York from 1959 to 1973.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-1) He was the leader of the moderate faction of his party, known as the Rockefeller Republicans.
After graduating from Dartmouth College in 1930, Rockefeller worked at various businesses connected to his family. He served as Assistant Secretary of State for American Republic Affairs for presidents Franklin D. Roosevelt and Harry S. Truman (1944–1945), and as Undersecretary of Health, Education and Welfare (HEW) under Dwight D. Eisenhower from 1953 to 1954. He was first elected governor of New York in 1958, and was re-elected in 1962, 1966, and 1970. As governor of New York, Rockefeller's achievements included the expansion of the State University of New York (SUNY), efforts to protect the environment, the construction of the Empire State Plaza in Albany, increased facilities and personnel for medical care, and the creation of the New York State Council on the Arts. Rockefeller was often considered to be liberal, progressive,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-2) or moderate. In an agreement that was termed the Treaty of Fifth Avenue, he persuaded Richard Nixon to alter the Republican Party platform just before the 1960 Republican National Convention.

After unsuccessfully seeking the Republican presidential nomination in 1960, 1964, and 1968, Rockefeller was appointed vice president of the United States by President Gerald Ford in December 1974. Rockefeller was the second vice president appointed to the position under the 25th Amendment, following Ford himself. Rockefeller did not seek a full term in the 1976 election with Ford, who named Kansas senator Bob Dole as his running mate instead of Rockefeller that year. Rockefeller retired from politics in 1977 and died two years later from a heart attack.
As a businessman, Rockefeller was president and later chair of [Rockefeller Center, Inc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Center,_Inc. "Rockefeller Center, Inc."). He also formed the International Basic Economy Corporation in 1947. Rockefeller assembled a significant art collection and promoted public access to the arts. He served as trustee, treasurer, and president of the Museum of Modern Art and founded the Museum of Primitive Art in 1954. In the area of philanthropy, he founded the Rockefeller Brothers Fund in 1940 with his four brothers and established the American International Association for Economic and Social Development in 1946.

## Early life and education (1908–1930)
Nelson Aldrich Rockefeller was born on July 8, 1908, in Bar Harbor, Maine.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris19607-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPersico198223-4) Named Nelson Aldrich after his maternal grandfather Nelson W. Aldrich,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPersico198223-4) he was the second son and third child of financier and philanthropist [John Davison Rockefeller Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_D._Rockefeller_Jr. "John D. Rockefeller Jr.") and philanthropist and socialite Abigail "Abby" Aldrich.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris19607-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPersico198223-4) He had two older siblings—Abby and John III—as well as three younger brothers: Laurance, Winthrop, and David.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPersico198224-5) His father, John Jr., was the only son of Standard Oil co-founder John D. Rockefeller and schoolteacher Laura Spelman.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPersico198223%E2%80%9324-6) His mother, Abby, was a daughter of Senator Nelson Wilmarth Aldrich and Abigail P. Greene.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-7)

**Nelson Aldrich Rockefeller** (July 8, 1908 – January 26, 1979) was the 41st vice president of the United States, serving from 1974 to 1977 under President Gerald Ford. A member of the Republican Party and the wealthy Rockefeller family, he was the 49th governor of New York from 1959 to 1973.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-1) He was the leader of the moderate faction of his party, known as the Rockefeller Republicans.
After graduating from Dartmouth College in 1930, Rockefeller worked at various businesses connected to his family. He served as Assistant Secretary of State for American Republic Affairs for presidents Franklin D. Roosevelt and Harry S. Truman (1944–1945), and as Undersecretary of Health, Education and Welfare (HEW) under Dwight D. Eisenhower from 1953 to 1954. He was first elected governor of New York in 1958, and was re-elected in 1962, 1966, and 1970. As governor of New York, Rockefeller's achievements included the expansion of the State University of New York (SUNY), efforts to protect the environment, the construction of the Empire State Plaza in Albany, increased facilities and personnel for medical care, and the creation of the New York State Council on the Arts. Rockefeller was often considered to be liberal, progressive,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-2) or moderate. In an agreement that was termed the Treaty of Fifth Avenue, he persuaded Richard Nixon to alter the Republican Party platform just before the 1960 Republican National Convention.
texts.2:
After unsuccessfully seeking the Republican presidential nomination in 1960, 1964, and 1968, Rockefeller was appointed vice president of the United States by President Gerald Ford in December 1974. Rockefeller was the second vice president appointed to the position under the 25th Amendment, following Ford himself. Rockefeller did not seek a full term in the 1976 election with Ford, who named Kansas senator Bob Dole as his running mate instead of Rockefeller that year. Rockefeller retired from politics in 1977 and died two years later from a heart attack.
As a businessman, Rockefeller was president and later chair of [Rockefeller Center, Inc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Center,_Inc. "Rockefeller Center, Inc."). He also formed the International Basic Economy Corporation in 1947. Rockefeller assembled a significant art collection and promoted public access to the arts. He served as trustee, treasurer, and president of the Museum of Modern Art and founded the Museum of Primitive Art in 1954. In the area of philanthropy, he founded the Rockefeller Brothers Fund in 1940 with his four brothers and established the American International Association for Economic and Social Development in 1946.

## Early life and education (1908–1930)
Nelson Aldrich Rockefeller was born on July 8, 1908, in Bar Harbor, Maine.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris19607-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPersico198223-4) Named Nelson Aldrich after his maternal grandfather Nelson W. Aldrich,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPersico198223-4) he was the second son and third child of financier and philanthropist [John Davison Rockefeller Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_D._Rockefeller_Jr. "John D. Rockefeller Jr.") and philanthropist and socialite Abigail "Abby" Aldrich.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris19607-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPersico198223-4) He had two older siblings—Abby and John III—as well as three younger brothers: Laurance, Winthrop, and David.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPersico198224-5) His father, John Jr., was the only son of Standard Oil co-founder John D. Rockefeller and schoolteacher Laura Spelman.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPersico198223%E2%80%9324-6) His mother, Abby, was a daughter of Senator Nelson Wilmarth Aldrich and Abigail P. Greene.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller#cite_note-7)

**Derek Anthony West** (born August 12, 1965) is an American attorney, former government official, and the senior vice president and chief legal officer of Uber.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-2) Before Uber, West was the 17th associate attorney general of the United States[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-3) and general counsel of PepsiCo.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-4) West previously served as the assistant attorney general of the Civil Division, the largest litigating division in the Department of Justice, and was the first African American to hold that position.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-5)

During his time at the Department of Justice, West played a role in the administration's decision to stop defending the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) after concluding that the statute was unconstitutional.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-6) West was also involved in efforts by the department to reclaim $37 billion from large financial institutions[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-7) and worked on the department's efforts to improve public safety in Indian country, including the tribal provisions in the 2013 reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-10) On August 21, 2014, West announced a $16.65 billion settlement with Bank of America to resolve federal and state claims against Bank of America including its existing and former subsidiaries, including Countrywide Financial Corporation and [Merrill Lynch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrill_Lynch_&_Co. "Merrill Lynch & Co.").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-12)
West is the brother-in-law of former Vice PresidentKamala Harris. He served as an advisor to her 2024 presidential campaign.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-:0-13)

## Early life and education
[edit]
West was born in San Francisco, California, the son of Margaret "Peggy" (née Reddick) and Franklin Delano West (1940–2013).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-WashingtonPostBio-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-16) West was raised in San Jose, California, where he lived with his two younger sisters, Pamela and Patricia.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-17) His father, the first person in his family to attend college, was born and raised in Georgia and worked for IBM while his mother, who was a teacher, was born and raised in Alabama.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-WashingtonPostBio-15)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-18) He attended Bellarmine College Preparatory, a Catholic, all-male, private secondary school, where he served as freshman class president, before graduating in 1983.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-WestBloomberg-19)

## Early life and education
West earned his Bachelor of Arts in government from Harvard College in 1987, where he served as publisher of the _Harvard Political Review_.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-20) In 1988, West began volunteering and working on political campaigns, engaging in Democratic political causes, such as working as the chief of staff to the Boston, Massachusetts treasurer of Michael Dukakis's presidential campaign.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-US_Senate_Judiciary_Questionnaire-21) West also served as a finance director to the Democratic Governors Association, until 1989.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-US_Senate_Judiciary_Questionnaire-21) He earned his Juris Doctor from Stanford Law School in 1992, where he served as the president of the _Stanford Law Review_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-22) While attending Stanford, he worked as a summer intern for Swidler Berlin Shereff Friedman in 1990.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-US_Senate_Judiciary_Questionnaire-21) He also worked as a summer intern for Tuttle & Taylor, and Morrison & Foerster in 1991.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-WashingtonPostBio-15)

**Derek Anthony West** (born August 12, 1965) is an American attorney, former government official, and the senior vice president and chief legal officer of Uber.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-2) Before Uber, West was the 17th associate attorney general of the United States[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-3) and general counsel of PepsiCo.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-4) West previously served as the assistant attorney general of the Civil Division, the largest litigating division in the Department of Justice, and was the first African American to hold that position.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-5)
texts.1:
During his time at the Department of Justice, West played a role in the administration's decision to stop defending the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) after concluding that the statute was unconstitutional.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-6) West was also involved in efforts by the department to reclaim $37 billion from large financial institutions[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-7) and worked on the department's efforts to improve public safety in Indian country, including the tribal provisions in the 2013 reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-10) On August 21, 2014, West announced a $16.65 billion settlement with Bank of America to resolve federal and state claims against Bank of America including its existing and former subsidiaries, including Countrywide Financial Corporation and [Merrill Lynch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrill_Lynch_&_Co. "Merrill Lynch & Co.").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-12)
West is the brother-in-law of former Vice PresidentKamala Harris. He served as an advisor to her 2024 presidential campaign.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-:0-13)
texts.2:
## Early life and education
[edit]
West was born in San Francisco, California, the son of Margaret "Peggy" (née Reddick) and Franklin Delano West (1940–2013).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-WashingtonPostBio-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-16) West was raised in San Jose, California, where he lived with his two younger sisters, Pamela and Patricia.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-17) His father, the first person in his family to attend college, was born and raised in Georgia and worked for IBM while his mother, who was a teacher, was born and raised in Alabama.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-WashingtonPostBio-15)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-18) He attended Bellarmine College Preparatory, a Catholic, all-male, private secondary school, where he served as freshman class president, before graduating in 1983.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-WestBloomberg-19)
texts.3:
## Early life and education
West earned his Bachelor of Arts in government from Harvard College in 1987, where he served as publisher of the _Harvard Political Review_.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-20) In 1988, West began volunteering and working on political campaigns, engaging in Democratic political causes, such as working as the chief of staff to the Boston, Massachusetts treasurer of Michael Dukakis's presidential campaign.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-US_Senate_Judiciary_Questionnaire-21) West also served as a finance director to the Democratic Governors Association, until 1989.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-US_Senate_Judiciary_Questionnaire-21) He earned his Juris Doctor from Stanford Law School in 1992, where he served as the president of the _Stanford Law Review_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-22) While attending Stanford, he worked as a summer intern for Swidler Berlin Shereff Friedman in 1990.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-US_Senate_Judiciary_Questionnaire-21) He also worked as a summer intern for Tuttle & Taylor, and Morrison & Foerster in 1991.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_West_(attorney)#cite_note-WashingtonPostBio-15)

## Ghana prosecutor charge ex-petroleum authority CEO, six odas ova alleged $28m extortion and money laundering scheme
Wia dis foto come from, Musthapha Abdul-Hamid/Facebook
Published 17 July 2025
Read am in 5 mins
Di office of special prosecutor (OSP) don formally charge ex-CEO of di national petroleum authority (NPA) and 6 odas for dia alleged role for one major alleged extortion and money laundering scheme.
Dem tok say dem charge oga Mustapha Abdul-Hamid, di former CEO and di oda staff and companies bifor di high court for Accra - e dey inside one statement from di prosecutor office.
**Dis na di list of di accused pipo**
*   Mustapha Abdul-Hamid - former CEO of di national petroleum authority (NPA)  
*   Jacob Kwamina Amuah - Coordinator for unified petroleum pricing fund/managing director for three companies (propnest, kel logistics and kings energy  
*   Wendy Newman - NPA staff  
*   Albert Ankrah - Kel logistics director  
*   Isaac Mensah - Kel logistics director  
*   Bright Bediako-Mensah - Kel logistics and Kings energy director  
*   Kwame Aboagye Acquah - Kings energy director  
*   Propnest limited  
*   Kel logistics limited  
*   Kings Energy limited
According to di special prosecutor, dem investigate dis mata since 2024 into wetin dem describe as "alleged unlawful conduct wey involve diversion of public funds and collusion wit oil marketing and bulk distribution companies."

## How di extortion and money laundering happun
Di special prosecutor tok say between 2022 and December 2024, di first three accused pipo - Mustapha Abdul-Hamid, Jacob Kwamina Amuah and Wendy Newman bin allegedly use dia official job for di national petroleum authority to operate criminal extortion scheme.
Di accused pipo bin use dis ogbonge scheme to allegedly collect GHc 280m ($27m) from petroleum transporters and oil marketing companies.
For dis scheme, di prosecutors office tok say di former CEO oga Mustapha Abdul-Hamid and di two oda staff (Jacob and Wendy) bin take advantage of dia position inside di NPA "without lawful mandate."
According to di OSP, oga Jacob Amuah bin allegedly carry GHC24m ($2.3m) give di former CEO Mustapha Hamid directly between January and December 2024.
"Dem bin carry additional GHC227.2m ($22m) through Wendy Newman under di direction of Jacob Amuah."
Di OSP add say "investigations don further show say di oda accused pipo - Albert Ankrah, Isaac Mensah, Bright Bediako Mensah and Kwaku Aboagye Acquah in collaboration wit anoda director for Kels Logistics, bin create wey dem use Propnest, Kel logistics and Kings energy, as vehicles for laundering di illegal moni."
Dem bin allegedly "use di moni to buy trucks for oil distribution business, dem also build fuel stations as part of di effort to hide and disguise di source of di criminal proceeds."
Di special prosecutor bin charge di individuals and di three companies wit 25 counts.

## Dis counts include
Wia dis foto come from, Musthapha Abdul-Hamid/Facebook
Wetin we call dis foto, Musthapha Abdul-Hamid
*   Extortion by public officer contrary to section 151 of di criminal offences act, 1960 (Act 29)  
*   Conspiracy to commit money laundering, contrary to section 23 of act 29 and sections 1(1), 1(2), and 4 of di anti-money laundering Act, 2020 (Act 1044)  
*   Money laundering, contrary to sections 1(1), 1(2) and 4 of Act 1044
According to di office of di special prosecutor, one pesin oga Osei Tutu Adjei wey be director for di ninth accused company, dey at large.
Di kontri dey pursue dis accused pipo wia dem go appear bifor court and dem go take dia plea.

## Wetin di former petroleum authority CEO tok
For February dis year, di special prosecutor oga Kissi Agyebeng for one press conference don tok say dem dey investigate di former petroleum authority boss ova dis mata.
Im tok say if dem finish dia investigation, dem go tok di pipo of Ghana wetin dem find.
But afta dat press conference, di ex - NPA boss Mustapha Abdul-Hamid write for im social media page say im go dey available for any investigation.
"As at dis afternoon (12 February 2025), I neva receive any invitation from any state investigation body, wey I neva dey under investigation for any alleged crime," Mustapha Abdul-Hamid tok.
Im add say "however, I dey willing to avail myself to assist for any investigation about di alleged embezzlement of funds."
Di OSP later don explain say dem neva dey tok pipo dem dey investigate say dem dey do investigation unless dem finish gathering dia information bifor dem go "put di facts bifor di suspects and accused pipo."

## Di ex-petroleum authority deny di fresh charges
For one statement on top im social media pages, di former petroleum authority boss Mustapha Abdul-Hamid tok say im neva do anytin wrong during im time as CEO of NPA between 2021 to 2024.
Dis na di tins im lawyers write for di statement im share on top im facebook.
*   Our client don deny all di allegation wey im go defend im name for court  
*   Di office of di special prosecutor bin invite our client on 25 February 2025 wey dem question am ova di allegations of mismanagement and procurement wahala  
*   Our client bin serve well for im tenure as NPA boss  
*   Di former NPA boss dey confidence say di truth of im innocence go prevail

## Company governance
Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) is the state-owned oil and gas company of Ghana, responsible for exploration, development, production and marketing of petroleum and natural gas resources in the country. Established in 1983, GNPC plays a central role in Ghana's oil and gas sector, which has become increasingly important to the country’s economy since the discovery of significant oil reserves in the mid-2000s.
GNPC’s upstream operations involve both direct exploration and production as well as partnerships with international oil companies (IOCs) through joint ventures and production-sharing agreements. Key oil fields in Ghana include the Jubilee field, TEN (Tweneboa, Enyenra, Ntomme) fields and the Sankofa Gye Nyame field, all located offshore in the Tano Basin and Deepwater Tano Cape Three Points areas.
GNPC also plays a significant role in natural gas production and commercialization, but has, in practice, ceded its role of gas aggregation and operation of the Western Corridor Gas Infrastructure Project to the Ghana Gas Company, which processes gas from Ghana’s offshore fields for domestic power generation.
Ghana’s refining sector is handled mainly by the Tema Oil Refinery, though GNPC has been exploring options for greater involvement in refining and petrochemical activities.
Ghana’s national oil company (NOC) is structured as a public limited company but operates as a state-owned enterprise and is not listed on a stock exchange. In the early years of its inception, GNPC’s primary role was to monitor and regulate the petroleum sector on behalf of the Ministry of Energy (Ghana Petroleum Regulatory Authority Bill 2008). This changed when additional oil and gas were discovered in the offshore Jubilee field. The prospect of greater participation in and revenues from the oil sector prompted the government to establish the Petroleum Commission in 2010 (the law was enacted in 2011) to take over regulatory duties from GNPC.
Joseph Abuabu Dazie, a former GNPC financial executive, has served as the CEO of GNPC since May 2024, when the former CEO Opoku-Ahweneeh Danquah resigned (17). The government of Ghana appoints the company’s board of directors, with members typically including government officials and industry professionals.

## Company governance
Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) is the state-owned oil and gas company of Ghana, responsible for exploration, development, production and marketing of petroleum and natural gas resources in the country. Established in 1983, GNPC plays a central role in Ghana's oil and gas sector, which has become increasingly important to the country’s economy since the discovery of significant oil reserves in the mid-2000s.
GNPC’s upstream operations involve both direct exploration and production as well as partnerships with international oil companies (IOCs) through joint ventures and production-sharing agreements. Key oil fields in Ghana include the Jubilee field, TEN (Tweneboa, Enyenra, Ntomme) fields and the Sankofa Gye Nyame field, all located offshore in the Tano Basin and Deepwater Tano Cape Three Points areas.
GNPC also plays a significant role in natural gas production and commercialization, but has, in practice, ceded its role of gas aggregation and operation of the Western Corridor Gas Infrastructure Project to the Ghana Gas Company, which processes gas from Ghana’s offshore fields for domestic power generation.
Ghana’s refining sector is handled mainly by the Tema Oil Refinery, though GNPC has been exploring options for greater involvement in refining and petrochemical activities.
Ghana’s national oil company (NOC) is structured as a public limited company but operates as a state-owned enterprise and is not listed on a stock exchange. In the early years of its inception, GNPC’s primary role was to monitor and regulate the petroleum sector on behalf of the Ministry of Energy (Ghana Petroleum Regulatory Authority Bill 2008). This changed when additional oil and gas were discovered in the offshore Jubilee field. The prospect of greater participation in and revenues from the oil sector prompted the government to establish the Petroleum Commission in 2010 (the law was enacted in 2011) to take over regulatory duties from GNPC.
Joseph Abuabu Dazie, a former GNPC financial executive, has served as the CEO of GNPC since May 2024, when the former CEO Opoku-Ahweneeh Danquah resigned (17). The government of Ghana appoints the company’s board of directors, with members typically including government officials and industry professionals.

## Ghana prosecutor charge ex-petroleum authority CEO, six odas ova alleged $28m extortion and money laundering scheme
Wia dis foto come from, Musthapha Abdul-Hamid/Facebook
Published 17 July 2025
Read am in 5 mins
Di office of special prosecutor (OSP) don formally charge ex-CEO of di national petroleum authority (NPA) and 6 odas for dia alleged role for one major alleged extortion and money laundering scheme.
Dem tok say dem charge oga Mustapha Abdul-Hamid, di former CEO and di oda staff and companies bifor di high court for Accra - e dey inside one statement from di prosecutor office.
**Dis na di list of di accused pipo**
*   Mustapha Abdul-Hamid - former CEO of di national petroleum authority (NPA)  
*   Jacob Kwamina Amuah - Coordinator for unified petroleum pricing fund/managing director for three companies (propnest, kel logistics and kings energy  
*   Wendy Newman - NPA staff  
*   Albert Ankrah - Kel logistics director  
*   Isaac Mensah - Kel logistics director  
*   Bright Bediako-Mensah - Kel logistics and Kings energy director  
*   Kwame Aboagye Acquah - Kings energy director  
*   Propnest limited  
*   Kel logistics limited  
*   Kings Energy limited
According to di special prosecutor, dem investigate dis mata since 2024 into wetin dem describe as "alleged unlawful conduct wey involve diversion of public funds and collusion wit oil marketing and bulk distribution companies."
texts.1:
## How di extortion and money laundering happun
Di special prosecutor tok say between 2022 and December 2024, di first three accused pipo - Mustapha Abdul-Hamid, Jacob Kwamina Amuah and Wendy Newman bin allegedly use dia official job for di national petroleum authority to operate criminal extortion scheme.
Di accused pipo bin use dis ogbonge scheme to allegedly collect GHc 280m ($27m) from petroleum transporters and oil marketing companies.
For dis scheme, di prosecutors office tok say di former CEO oga Mustapha Abdul-Hamid and di two oda staff (Jacob and Wendy) bin take advantage of dia position inside di NPA "without lawful mandate."
According to di OSP, oga Jacob Amuah bin allegedly carry GHC24m ($2.3m) give di former CEO Mustapha Hamid directly between January and December 2024.
"Dem bin carry additional GHC227.2m ($22m) through Wendy Newman under di direction of Jacob Amuah."
Di OSP add say "investigations don further show say di oda accused pipo - Albert Ankrah, Isaac Mensah, Bright Bediako Mensah and Kwaku Aboagye Acquah in collaboration wit anoda director for Kels Logistics, bin create wey dem use Propnest, Kel logistics and Kings energy, as vehicles for laundering di illegal moni."
Dem bin allegedly "use di moni to buy trucks for oil distribution business, dem also build fuel stations as part of di effort to hide and disguise di source of di criminal proceeds."
Di special prosecutor bin charge di individuals and di three companies wit 25 counts.
texts.2:
## Dis counts include
Wia dis foto come from, Musthapha Abdul-Hamid/Facebook
Wetin we call dis foto, Musthapha Abdul-Hamid
*   Extortion by public officer contrary to section 151 of di criminal offences act, 1960 (Act 29)  
*   Conspiracy to commit money laundering, contrary to section 23 of act 29 and sections 1(1), 1(2), and 4 of di anti-money laundering Act, 2020 (Act 1044)  
*   Money laundering, contrary to sections 1(1), 1(2) and 4 of Act 1044
According to di office of di special prosecutor, one pesin oga Osei Tutu Adjei wey be director for di ninth accused company, dey at large.
Di kontri dey pursue dis accused pipo wia dem go appear bifor court and dem go take dia plea.
texts.3:
## Wetin di former petroleum authority CEO tok
For February dis year, di special prosecutor oga Kissi Agyebeng for one press conference don tok say dem dey investigate di former petroleum authority boss ova dis mata.
Im tok say if dem finish dia investigation, dem go tok di pipo of Ghana wetin dem find.
But afta dat press conference, di ex - NPA boss Mustapha Abdul-Hamid write for im social media page say im go dey available for any investigation.
"As at dis afternoon (12 February 2025), I neva receive any invitation from any state investigation body, wey I neva dey under investigation for any alleged crime," Mustapha Abdul-Hamid tok.
Im add say "however, I dey willing to avail myself to assist for any investigation about di alleged embezzlement of funds."
Di OSP later don explain say dem neva dey tok pipo dem dey investigate say dem dey do investigation unless dem finish gathering dia information bifor dem go "put di facts bifor di suspects and accused pipo."
texts.4:
## Di ex-petroleum authority deny di fresh charges
For one statement on top im social media pages, di former petroleum authority boss Mustapha Abdul-Hamid tok say im neva do anytin wrong during im time as CEO of NPA between 2021 to 2024.
Dis na di tins im lawyers write for di statement im share on top im facebook.
*   Our client don deny all di allegation wey im go defend im name for court  
*   Di office of di special prosecutor bin invite our client on 25 February 2025 wey dem question am ova di allegations of mismanagement and procurement wahala  
*   Our client bin serve well for im tenure as NPA boss  
*   Di former NPA boss dey confidence say di truth of im innocence go prevail

## Who We Are
### Chris Lyons
BEA Advisory Board & President Web3 Media, a16z crypto
Christopher Lyons is President, Web3 Media at a16z crypto. Prior to joining the team at a16z crypto, he co-founded the firm’s Cultural Leadership Fund (CLF) and was instrumental in launching the first Seed Fund. Lyons started his career in the music industry working for Grammy-Award-winning producer Jermaine Dupri as a sound engineer. He then launched his first startup, a mobile app and digital menu offering called PictureMenu. Lyons joined a16z in 2013, first as chief of staff to co-founder Ben Horowitz.

## Who We Are
### Kwasi Mitchell
Chief Purpose and DEI Officer, Deloitte
Kwasi Mitchell is the chief purpose officer at Deloitte. He is responsible for leading the organization-wide strategy that powers Deloitte’s commitment to purpose and drives a broader impact for our clients, people and the communities in which we live and work. Kwasi built and oversees the organization’s first dedicated Purpose Office focused on addressing some of the world’s most complex societal issues including diversity, equity and inclusion, sustainability and climate change, education and workforce development, and technology trust ethics. In his role, Kwasi creates pathways of opportunity for our people and clients to find purpose in their work and harness their skills to drive a collective impact that addresses systemic societal issues. His belief in the power of a purpose-driven organization has led Deloitte to strategically invest $1.5 billion over 10 years to address equity for those facing the greatest barriers to prosperity and his passion for creating a more equitable society has earned him a board seat on several national and global nonprofits. Kwasi’s leadership brings focus to the shared impact and lasting change we can have on society at large when we put our purpose into action and embrace the differences that unite us. Prior to being named Deloitte’s chief purpose officer, Kwasi was the diversity, equity and inclusion leader, the pro bono and social impact lead for Deloitte’s 50,000+ person Consulting practice and served as the Strategy Offering leader for Deloitte’s Government & Public Services practice where he advised clients within both the government and commercial sectors. His insights of building a purpose-driven organization have been featured in Fast Company, Forbes, Business Insider, Fortune and more. Kwasi has a PhD in inorganic chemistry from Northwestern University, an MBA from Drexel University and sits on the board of several national and global nonprofits focused on building a more equitable society. He lives in Washington, D.C. where he spends time with his lovely wife, Kathleen.

## Who We Are
### Marc H. Morial
President and CEO, National Urban League
Marc Morial, one of the few national leaders to possess “street smarts,” and “boardroom savvy,” is the transformative President and CEO of the National Urban League, the nation’s largest historic civil rights and urban advocacy organization. He served as the highly successful and popular Mayor of New Orleans as well as the President of the U.S. Conference of Mayors. Marc previously was a Louisiana State Senator and was a lawyer in New Orleans with an active, high-profile practice. He is a leading voice on the national stage in the battle for jobs, education, housing, health, voting rights, equity, and entrepreneurship. Marc is a published author; his leadership book, Gumbo Coalition: 10 Leadership Lessons That Help You Inspire, United, and Achieve has been widely acclaimed, and his column entitled To Be Equal, reaches hundreds of thousands. He is the host of the weekly syndicated television show, America’s Black Forum. A graduate of Georgetown University Law Center, and the University of Pennsylvania with a degree in Economics and African American Studies, he has been recognized as one of the 100 most influential Black Americans by Ebony Magazine, one of the top 50 Non-Profit Leaders by the Non-Profit Times, one of the 100 Most Influential Black Lawyers in America and he has also been inducted into the International Civil Rights Walk of Fame in Atlanta, GA. Marc and his father, the late Ernest “Dutch” Morial, are history makers as the first African American father/son mayors in the U.S. and were the subject of a Double Jeopardy question on the legendary Jeopardy television game show in the 1990s.

## Who We Are
### Michael Neal
Senior Fellow, Urban Institute
Michael Neal is a Senior Fellow in the Housing Finance Policy Center at the Urban Institute. Mr. Neal’s research intersects racial equity, homeownership, and wealth building. **Richard Rhoads**, former CEO of New England Business Service, Inc. (NEBS), Dies at 96
Richard H. Rhoads, former president, chief executive officer and chairman of Groton-based New England Business Service, Inc. (NEBS), died Wednesday, April 8, 2026 after a brief illness. Richard, of Duxbury and West Falmouth, leaves his wife, Margaret, of 63 years; his daughter, Virginia, and son-in-law, John McConnell of Whidbey Island, WA; his son, Christopher, daughter-in-law, Emily Paddon Rhoads and three grandchildren, Roscoe, George and Josey of Swarthmore, PA; and his daughter Jennifer of Portland, OR.
Richard was born on January 23, 1930 in Philadelphia, the youngest of three children. His father, Jay Roscoe Rhoads, co-headed the family firm in the wholesale textile business, while his mother, Mary Grace Rudolph, cared for their home and family.
He attended the Haverford School, in Haverford, PA, and the University of Virginia, where he majored in History, served in the Reserve Officer Training Corps and was commissioned a U.S. Army second lieutenant upon graduation in 1952, while the Korean War was underway. He was sent first to Fort Lawton in Seattle where he showed natural management skills in his running of the Officers Club.
Deployed to Japan, Richard, 23, served as company commander in an amphibious support regiment, responsible for about 100 troops. He was honorably discharged in August 1954 as first lieutenant.
Rather than enter the family textile business in Philadelphia, where his older brother Jay worked with their father, Richard looked elsewhere for companies with well-regarded training programs. He landed as a salesman in the Chicago office of Armstrong Cork Co., a ceiling-tile company.
In 1960, Richard left Armstrong to enter the Graduate School of Business at Columbia University, an unusual move at the time for a 30-year-old on the rise at a successful company. Richard made the Dean’s List and was elected president of the student body.

In 1963, he married Margaret Haines Whitall, also from Philadelphia and a graduate of Germantown Friends School and Wheaton College in Massachusetts. Margaret had worked as a program director at the Center for International Visitors in Philadelphia.
A year later, the newlywed couple had their first of three children, Virginia. Richard could walk to work at management consulting firm Arthur D. Little, Inc. in midtown Manhattan.
Richard began hearing at this time from his older brother Jay about NEBS.
Jay had joined the company, founded in 1951 by Al Anderson, in 1955 as vice president and treasurer. The company produced business forms—such as receipts, invoices and labels—and sold them by mail to small businesses. At his brother’s urging, Richard in 1965 left the big city corporate world for the promising start-up in rural Massachusetts, headquartered first in Townsend and later in Groton at 500 Main Street.
He succeeded his brother as president in 1971 and four years later as chief executive officer. Sales grew by 25% or more annually through these years, reaching $50 million by the end of the decade. The rapid growth led to additional production plants in New Hampshire, Missouri, Arizona, as well as in Canada and the U.K.
“Richard took over what was an opportunistic marketing effort and developed it into a powerful and predictable machine,” Jay said in a company history.
In four out of five years through the 1980s, _Forbes Magazine_ named NEBS one of the 200 best small companies in America, earning a spot in 1988 on its honor role of 17 companies. _The Boston Globe_ in 1989 honored NEBS on its list of top 10 companies in Massachusetts.
By the time Richard stepped down as CEO in 1991, the company had more than $230 million in sales and 2,000 employees. He retired as chairman in 1995, the year the company listed its shares on the New York Stock Exchange. He continued to serve on the board of directors until 2000. In 2004, Deluxe Corp., a supplier of products and services for small businesses, acquired the company. The Groton location is now poised for residential development.

“Richard has represented the fine human and business qualities that all people associated with NEBS came to expect when they heard the name Rhoads,” said Bob Murray, who in 1995 became president, CEO and chairman of NEBS.
Richard relished his annual fly-fishing trips with close friends to places like Alaska, Labrador and Montana. In retirement, Richard and Margaret moved from Groton to Boston’s Back Bay, where they became regulars at the Boston Symphony Orchestra, and to Carefree, AZ., where Richard worked diligently on his golf game.
Richard’s life will be celebrated in a private ceremony on Cape Cod, where his family has spent summers since the late 1960s. In lieu of flowers, please make a donation in his memory to the Buzzards Bay Coalition, www.savebuzzardsbay.org

**Frank Leonard VanderSloot**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-LandReport-1) (born August 14, 1948) is an American entrepreneur, radio network owner, rancher, and political campaign financier. He is the founder and former chief executive officer of Melaleuca, Inc.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Berman-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-inc-3) His other business interests include the Riverbend Ranch[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Ranch1-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Ranch3-5) and Riverbend Communications.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Radio1-6) VanderSloot also serves on the board of directors and executive board of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Chamber1-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Popkey-8)In 2011,_The Land Report_ listed him as the nation's 92nd largest landowner.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-LandReport-1) In 2017, Forbes listed VanderSloot as the richest person in Idaho and the 302nd wealthiest American with a net worth of $2.7 billion.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Wealth-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-10)

VanderSloot served as a national finance co-chair for Mitt Romney's presidential campaigns in 2008 and 2012.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Murphy-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-NYT1-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-13) He contributed $1.1 million and helped to raise between $2 million and $5 million for Romney's 2012 campaign.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-motherjones-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Vogel1-15) He is a significant financial contributor to Republican presidential candidates and Idaho political campaigns.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-16) He has also paid for advertising in opposition to several Idaho Democratic political candidates. VanderSloot is the primary financier of the American Heritage Charter School in Idaho Falls.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-VanDerSlootFarms-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-VanderSloot-Funded-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-IdahoFallsCharter-19)

## Early life and education
[edit]
VanderSloot was born on August 14, 1948,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-21) to Peter Francis (Frank) VanderSloot (1913–1982) and Margaret May Christensen Sindberg-Woodley VanderSloot (1915–2004).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-22) The family lived in Sheridan, Wyoming, and Hardin, Montana, before moving in 1949 to Cocolalla, Idaho, where they lived on a ranch. The elder VanderSloot worked as a painter for the Northern Pacific Railway.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-MargaretObit-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Carlson2-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-FrankDiscussion-25):57

## Early life and education
Frank VanderSloot graduated from Sandpoint High School in 1966.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-26) At the age of 16, he joined the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church), and later studied at Brigham Young University in Provo, Utah, where he worked and lived as a cleaner at a laundromat.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-ForbesLaundromat-27) After two semesters, he left school to serve a two-and-a-half-year LDS Mission in the Netherlands.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-ForbesLaundromat-27)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Popkey-8)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-28) Following his mission, he earned an [associate's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associate's_degree "Associate's degree") in business at Ricks College in Rexburg, Idaho. He then returned to Brigham Young University, where he earned a [bachelor's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in marketing in 1972.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-FrankDiscussion-25)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-SandpointPlasterInterview-29)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-ForbesLaundromat-27)

## Early life and education
After graduating from college, VanderSloot worked for 9 1⁄2 years at Automatic Data Processing in three cities. He first worked in sales and marketing before moving to general management and operations.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Carlson2-24)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Carlson-30) He left ADP to work as regional vice president at Cox Communications in Vancouver, Washington.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-FrankDiscussion-25):58[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Bonanza-31)

## Who We Are
### Kwasi Mitchell
Chief Purpose and DEI Officer, Deloitte
Kwasi Mitchell is the chief purpose officer at Deloitte. He is responsible for leading the organization-wide strategy that powers Deloitte’s commitment to purpose and drives a broader impact for our clients, people and the communities in which we live and work. Kwasi built and oversees the organization’s first dedicated Purpose Office focused on addressing some of the world’s most complex societal issues including diversity, equity and inclusion, sustainability and climate change, education and workforce development, and technology trust ethics. In his role, Kwasi creates pathways of opportunity for our people and clients to find purpose in their work and harness their skills to drive a collective impact that addresses systemic societal issues. His belief in the power of a purpose-driven organization has led Deloitte to strategically invest $1.5 billion over 10 years to address equity for those facing the greatest barriers to prosperity and his passion for creating a more equitable society has earned him a board seat on several national and global nonprofits. Kwasi’s leadership brings focus to the shared impact and lasting change we can have on society at large when we put our purpose into action and embrace the differences that unite us. Prior to being named Deloitte’s chief purpose officer, Kwasi was the diversity, equity and inclusion leader, the pro bono and social impact lead for Deloitte’s 50,000+ person Consulting practice and served as the Strategy Offering leader for Deloitte’s Government & Public Services practice where he advised clients within both the government and commercial sectors. His insights of building a purpose-driven organization have been featured in Fast Company, Forbes, Business Insider, Fortune and more. Kwasi has a PhD in inorganic chemistry from Northwestern University, an MBA from Drexel University and sits on the board of several national and global nonprofits focused on building a more equitable society. He lives in Washington, D.C. where he spends time with his lovely wife, Kathleen.

## Who We Are
### Marc H. Morial
President and CEO, National Urban League
Marc Morial, one of the few national leaders to possess “street smarts,” and “boardroom savvy,” is the transformative President and CEO of the National Urban League, the nation’s largest historic civil rights and urban advocacy organization. He served as the highly successful and popular Mayor of New Orleans as well as the President of the U.S. Conference of Mayors. Marc previously was a Louisiana State Senator and was a lawyer in New Orleans with an active, high-profile practice. He is a leading voice on the national stage in the battle for jobs, education, housing, health, voting rights, equity, and entrepreneurship. Marc is a published author; his leadership book, Gumbo Coalition: 10 Leadership Lessons That Help You Inspire, United, and Achieve has been widely acclaimed, and his column entitled To Be Equal, reaches hundreds of thousands. He is the host of the weekly syndicated television show, America’s Black Forum. A graduate of Georgetown University Law Center, and the University of Pennsylvania with a degree in Economics and African American Studies, he has been recognized as one of the 100 most influential Black Americans by Ebony Magazine, one of the top 50 Non-Profit Leaders by the Non-Profit Times, one of the 100 Most Influential Black Lawyers in America and he has also been inducted into the International Civil Rights Walk of Fame in Atlanta, GA. Marc and his father, the late Ernest “Dutch” Morial, are history makers as the first African American father/son mayors in the U.S. and were the subject of a Double Jeopardy question on the legendary Jeopardy television game show in the 1990s.

At his brother’s urging, Richard in 1965 left the big city corporate world for the promising start-up in rural Massachusetts, headquartered first in Townsend and later in Groton at 500 Main Street.
He succeeded his brother as president in 1971 and four years later as chief executive officer. Sales grew by 25% or more annually through these years, reaching $50 million by the end of the decade. The rapid growth led to additional production plants in New Hampshire, Missouri, Arizona, as well as in Canada and the U.K.
“Richard took over what was an opportunistic marketing effort and developed it into a powerful and predictable machine,” Jay said in a company history.
In four out of five years through the 1980s, _Forbes Magazine_ named NEBS one of the 200 best small companies in America, earning a spot in 1988 on its honor role of 17 companies. _The Boston Globe_ in 1989 honored NEBS on its list of top 10 companies in Massachusetts.
By the time Richard stepped down as CEO in 1991, the company had more than $230 million in sales and 2,000 employees. He retired as chairman in 1995, the year the company listed its shares on the New York Stock Exchange. He continued to serve on the board of directors until 2000. In 2004, Deluxe Corp., a supplier of products and services for small businesses, acquired the company. The Groton location is now poised for residential development.
texts.2:
“Richard has represented the fine human and business qualities that all people associated with NEBS came to expect when they heard the name Rhoads,” said Bob Murray, who in 1995 became president, CEO and chairman of NEBS.
Richard relished his annual fly-fishing trips with close friends to places like Alaska, Labrador and Montana. In retirement, Richard and Margaret moved from Groton to Boston’s Back Bay, where they became regulars at the Boston Symphony Orchestra, and to Carefree, AZ., where Richard worked diligently on his golf game.
Richard’s life will be celebrated in a private ceremony on Cape Cod, where his family has spent summers since the late 1960s. In lieu of flowers, please make a donation in his memory to the Buzzards Bay Coalition, www.savebuzzardsbay.org

texts.1: **Frank Leonard VanderSloot**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-LandReport-1) (born August 14, 1948) is an American entrepreneur, radio network owner, rancher, and political campaign financier. He is the founder and former chief executive officer of Melaleuca, Inc.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Berman-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-inc-3) His other business interests include the Riverbend Ranch[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Ranch1-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Ranch3-5) and Riverbend Communications.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Radio1-6) VanderSloot also serves on the board of directors and executive board of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Chamber1-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Popkey-8)In 2011,_The Land Report_ listed him as the nation's 92nd largest landowner.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-LandReport-1) In 2017, Forbes listed VanderSloot as the richest person in Idaho and the 302nd wealthiest American with a net worth of $2.7 billion.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Wealth-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-10)
texts.2: VanderSloot served as a national finance co-chair for Mitt Romney's presidential campaigns in 2008 and 2012.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Murphy-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-NYT1-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-13) He contributed $1.1 million and helped to raise between $2 million and $5 million for Romney's 2012 campaign.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-motherjones-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Vogel1-15) He is a significant financial contributor to Republican presidential candidates and Idaho political campaigns.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-16) He has also paid for advertising in opposition to several Idaho Democratic political candidates. VanderSloot is the primary financier of the American Heritage Charter School in Idaho Falls.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-VanDerSlootFarms-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-VanderSloot-Funded-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-IdahoFallsCharter-19)
texts.3:
## Early life and education
[edit]
VanderSloot was born on August 14, 1948,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-21) to Peter Francis (Frank) VanderSloot (1913–1982) and Margaret May Christensen Sindberg-Woodley VanderSloot (1915–2004).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-22) The family lived in Sheridan, Wyoming, and Hardin, Montana, before moving in 1949 to Cocolalla, Idaho, where they lived on a ranch. The elder VanderSloot worked as a painter for the Northern Pacific Railway.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-MargaretObit-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Carlson2-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-FrankDiscussion-25):57
texts.4:
## Early life and education
Frank VanderSloot graduated from Sandpoint High School in 1966.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-26) At the age of 16, he joined the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church), and later studied at Brigham Young University in Provo, Utah, where he worked and lived as a cleaner at a laundromat.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-ForbesLaundromat-27) After two semesters, he left school to serve a two-and-a-half-year LDS Mission in the Netherlands.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-ForbesLaundromat-27)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Popkey-8)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-28) Following his mission, he earned an [associate's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associate's_degree "Associate's degree") in business at Ricks College in Rexburg, Idaho. He then returned to Brigham Young University, where he earned a [bachelor's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in marketing in 1972.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-FrankDiscussion-25)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-SandpointPlasterInterview-29)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-ForbesLaundromat-27)
texts.5:
## Early life and education
After graduating from college, VanderSloot worked for 9 1⁄2 years at Automatic Data Processing in three cities. He first worked in sales and marketing before moving to general management and operations.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Carlson2-24)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Carlson-30) He left ADP to work as regional vice president at Cox Communications in Vancouver, Washington.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-FrankDiscussion-25):58[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_VanderSloot#cite_note-Bonanza-31)

**Alexander Kofi-Mensah Mould** is a Ghanaian politician and banker who is a former chief executive officer of Ghana National Petroleum Corporation.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:0-2) He is a member of the National Democratic Congress.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:1-3) Before he was appointed CEO of GNPC, he was the CEO of National Petroleum Authority.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-4)

## Early life and education
[edit]
Alex Mould's parents were W. J. Kwesi Mould of Jamestown, Accra and Felicia Awurafua Gsell of Ejuratia in Kwabre, Ashanti.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-5) W. J. Mould was a businessman and a nationalist who was active in Ghana's pre-independence movements, and had attended the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester as a representative of the Gold Coast Farmers Association.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-6) In 1947, W. J. Mould was the second individual after George Grant to make a financial contribution for the formation of the United Gold Coast Convention. Alex's sister, Betty Mould-Iddrisu, has served in government as Minister for Education and also Attorney-General and Minister for Justice.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-7)
Mould attended Accra Academy from 1973 to 1978 and Accra High School from 1978 to 1980 for O-Level and A-Level qualifications respectively. Mould's father died and was buried in 1980.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-8) He proceeded to the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology. There, he earned a bachelor of science degree in 1985 in chemical engineering.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:0-2) Mould enrolled at the College of Petroleum Studies, Oxford where he obtained a postgraduate diploma in Oil Marketing and Economics in 1989.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:1-3) In 1994, Mould earned a Master of Business Administration degree in Finance, Accounting and Decision Science from J. L. Kellogg Graduate School, Northwestern University, Illinois.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:0-2)

## Early life and education
After graduating from Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Mould was posted to undergo a one-year national service at the newly created Ghana National Petroleum Corporation in 1985.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:1-3)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:2-9) After service, he was employed by the corporation as a chemical engineer. He rose through the ranks to become a special assistant to the CEO of GNPC in the area of marketing.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:0-2)
In 1997, Mould resigned from GNPC and was appointed as a senior associate, Structured Trade Finance Americas of UBS Investment Bank from 1997 to 1999.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:1-3)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:3-10) He moved banks and was employed as associate director of Commodity Finance at Standard Chartered Bank in New York from 1999 to 2001. Mould was moved to the Ghana branch of Standard Chartered Bank in 2001 as executive director and co-head of the wholesale department.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:1-3) He remained in this role until his exit in 2008.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:0-2)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:2-9)

## National appointments
[edit]
When the John Atta Mills administration was voted into power in 2009, Mould was appointed chief executive officer of the National Petroleum Authority.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:0-2) He remained in the position till 2012.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:4-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:5-12) In January 2013, when the John Dramani Mahama administration took over the reins of government, Mould was sent to the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation as its chief executive.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:4-11)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-13)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:3-10) He took over from Nana Boakye Asafu Adjaye, who had headed the corporation since 2009.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:2-9)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:5-12) He remained in the position till the end of the John Mahama administration. In January 2017, he was replaced by Kofi Koduah Sarpong.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:3-10)
Mould is a brother to Betty Mould-Iddrisu a former Minister of Justice under the John Atta Mills administration and a former Minister of Education under the John Dramani Mahama administration.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-15) He lost his daughter, Naa Densua to Malaria on 1 January 2020. This was when she was on holiday in Mauritius.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-16)

WED, 04 JAN 2017 2
Information gathered by **Citi Business News** indicates that Dr. Kofi Kodua Sarpong will be taking over from Mr. Alex Mould as the Chief Executive Officer(CEO) of the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation(GNPC).
Mr. K.K Sarpong who was the former CEO of the Tema Oil Refinery (TOR) was appointed as the Executive Chairman of Asante Kotoko FC in 2010, but resigned in 2013.
He was until July 31, 2012 the Executive Chairman of Finatec Limited a consortium of Chartered Accountants, Lawyers and Investment Experts.
He had previously worked as the Deputy Managing Director and subsequently as the Managing Director of Tema Oil Refinery Limited from September 2003 to August 2009.
Dr. Sarpong garnered his International working experience with International Cocoa Organization as the Head of Administration and Financial Services Division from January 1999 to 2003.
At the Ghana Cocoa Board, Dr. Sarpong worked as Deputy Chief Executive (Finance and Administration) from 1994 to December 1998.
He worked with Produce Buying Company Limited as the Deputy Managing Director (Finance and Administration) from July 1990 to August 1994.
At Ghana Food Distribution Corporation, Dr. Sarpong worked in various capacities as Deputy Chief Accountant, Accountant and General Manager (Finance and Administration).

He also holds an MBA in Accounting and B.Sc (Administration) Accounting Option from University of Ghana Legon.

**Alexander Kofi-Mensah Mould** is a Ghanaian politician and banker who is a former chief executive officer of Ghana National Petroleum Corporation.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:0-2) He is a member of the National Democratic Congress.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:1-3) Before he was appointed CEO of GNPC, he was the CEO of National Petroleum Authority.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-4)
texts.1:
## Early life and education
[edit]
Alex Mould's parents were W. J. Kwesi Mould of Jamestown, Accra and Felicia Awurafua Gsell of Ejuratia in Kwabre, Ashanti.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-5) W. J. Mould was a businessman and a nationalist who was active in Ghana's pre-independence movements, and had attended the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester as a representative of the Gold Coast Farmers Association.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-6) In 1947, W. J. Mould was the second individual after George Grant to make a financial contribution for the formation of the United Gold Coast Convention. Alex's sister, Betty Mould-Iddrisu, has served in government as Minister for Education and also Attorney-General and Minister for Justice.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-7)
Mould attended Accra Academy from 1973 to 1978 and Accra High School from 1978 to 1980 for O-Level and A-Level qualifications respectively. Mould's father died and was buried in 1980.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-8) He proceeded to the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology. There, he earned a bachelor of science degree in 1985 in chemical engineering.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:0-2) Mould enrolled at the College of Petroleum Studies, Oxford where he obtained a postgraduate diploma in Oil Marketing and Economics in 1989.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:1-3) In 1994, Mould earned a Master of Business Administration degree in Finance, Accounting and Decision Science from J. L. Kellogg Graduate School, Northwestern University, Illinois.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:0-2)
texts.2:
## Early life and education
After graduating from Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Mould was posted to undergo a one-year national service at the newly created Ghana National Petroleum Corporation in 1985.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:1-3)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:2-9) After service, he was employed by the corporation as a chemical engineer. He rose through the ranks to become a special assistant to the CEO of GNPC in the area of marketing.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:0-2)
In 1997, Mould resigned from GNPC and was appointed as a senior associate, Structured Trade Finance Americas of UBS Investment Bank from 1997 to 1999.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:1-3)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:3-10) He moved banks and was employed as associate director of Commodity Finance at Standard Chartered Bank in New York from 1999 to 2001. Mould was moved to the Ghana branch of Standard Chartered Bank in 2001 as executive director and co-head of the wholesale department.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:1-3) He remained in this role until his exit in 2008.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:0-2)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:2-9)
texts.3:
## National appointments
[edit]
When the John Atta Mills administration was voted into power in 2009, Mould was appointed chief executive officer of the National Petroleum Authority.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:0-2) He remained in the position till 2012.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:4-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:5-12) In January 2013, when the John Dramani Mahama administration took over the reins of government, Mould was sent to the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation as its chief executive.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:4-11)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-13)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:3-10) He took over from Nana Boakye Asafu Adjaye, who had headed the corporation since 2009.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:2-9)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:5-12) He remained in the position till the end of the John Mahama administration. In January 2017, he was replaced by Kofi Koduah Sarpong.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-:3-10)
Mould is a brother to Betty Mould-Iddrisu a former Minister of Justice under the John Atta Mills administration and a former Minister of Education under the John Dramani Mahama administration.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-15) He lost his daughter, Naa Densua to Malaria on 1 January 2020. This was when she was on holiday in Mauritius.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mould#cite_note-16)
